body: This blog contains step-by-step solutions to the PortSwigger Web Security Academy access control labs. The labs cover a range of access control vulnerabilities, including unprotected admin panels, parameter-based role and user ID control, IDOR, and URL, method and referer bypasses. Each solution includes the Burp requests used to exploit the vulnerability. Basic Overview What is Access Control? Access control is a security mechanism that restricts access to resources based on the identity and permissions of the user. It ensures that only authorized users can access certain functionalities or data within an application. Broken access control occurs when an application fails to enforce these restrictions properly, allowing unauthorized users to access sensitive information or perform actions they shouldn't be able to. Preventing broken access control is crucial for maintaining the security and integrity of web applications. It involves implementing proper authentication and authorization mechanisms, validating user input, and regularly testing for vulnerabilities. It's located at an unpredictable location, but the location is disclosed somewhere in the application. Solve the lab by accessing the admin panel, and using it to delete the user carlos. To solve the lab, find the GUID for carlos, then submit his API key as the solution. You can log in to your own account using the following credentials: wiener:peter Solution: --- Lab: User ID controlled by request parameter with data leakage in redirect This lab contains an access control vulnerability where sensitive information is leaked in the body of a redirect response. To solve the lab, obtain the API key for the user carlos and submit it as the solution. You can log in to your own account using the following credentials: wiener:peter Solution: --- Lab: User ID controlled by request parameter with password disclosure This lab has user account page that contains the current user's existing password, prefilled in a masked input. To solve the lab, retrieve the administrator's password, then use it to delete the user carlos. You can log in to your own account using the following credentials: wiener:peter Solution: --- Lab: Insecure direct object references This lab stores user chat logs directly on the server's file system, and retrieves them using static URLs. Solve the lab by finding the password for the user carlos, and logging into their account. Solution: --- PRACTITIONER Lab: URL-based access control can be circumvented This website has an unauthenticated admin panel at /admin, but a front-end system has been configured to block external access to that path. However, the back-end application is built on a framework that supports the X-Original-URL header. To solve the lab, access the admin panel and delete the user carlos. Solution: --- Lab: Method-based access control can be circumvented This lab implements access controls based partly on the HTTP method of requests. You can familiarize yourself with the admin panel by logging in using the credentials administrator:admin. To solve the lab, log in using the credentials wiener:peter and exploit the flawed access controls to promote yourself to become an administrator. Solution: --- Lab: Multi-step process with no access control on one step This lab has an admin panel with a flawed multi-step process for changing a user's role. You can familiarize yourself with the admin panel by logging in using the credentials administrator:admin. To solve the lab, log in using the credentials wiener:peter and exploit the flawed access controls to promote yourself to become an administrator. Solution: --- Lab: Referer-based access control This lab controls access to certain admin functionality based on the Referer header. You can familiarize yourself with the admin panel by logging in using the credentials administrator:admin. body: Overview Nexus is a solid easy-rated box that chains together credential leakage through version control history, a real-world CRM RCE, and a creative abuse of an automated root-level sync job driven by attacker-controlled Git object paths. The key takeaway is that any process extracting file paths from Git metadata — or any user-controlled source — must treat those paths as untrusted input and strictly validate them before joining them onto a filesystem destination. | Stage | Technique | | ------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | Recon | Nmap scan, vhost fuzzing | | Initial Information | Gitea commit history leaking CRM database credentials | | Foothold | CVE-2026-38526 — Krayin CRM authenticated arbitrary file upload / RCE | | User (jones) | Password reuse of the leaked database credential | | Root | Path traversal in a root-owned systemd timer (template-sync.py) via a crafted Gitea template repository, used to plant an SSH key in /root/.ssh/authorized_keys | --- Machine Info: --- Recon I started with a standard Nmap service scan against the target. Only two ports are open, so port 80 was the clear starting point. Since the service redirected to nexus.htb, I added the host to my /etc/hosts file before continuing. nexus.htb Browsing the site manually, I looked for functional flaws and any information disclosure. On the careers page I found a contact email address, j.matthew@nexus.htb, which I noted down as it could be useful later in the enumeration process. Subdomain Fuzzing With a single vhost enumerated, I fuzzed for additional subdomains using ffuf. This uncovered two additional virtual hosts: git.nexus.htb and billing.nexus.htb. Both were added to /etc/hosts for further enumeration. billing.nexus.htb billing.nexus.htb revealed a Krayin CRM login page. Without valid credentials at this point, I moved on to the Git instance to see if it exposed anything useful. git.nexus.htb Under the Explore tab I found a single repository, admin/krayin-docker-setup, and two registered users: admin and jones. The repository contained three files and two commits. Reviewing the commit history, I found that commit 9b817fa4e0 had exposed credentials. Combining this leaked password with the email address I found earlier (j.matthew@nexus.htb), I was able to authenticate to billing.nexus.htb. --- Initial Foothold Authenticating to Krayin CRM Using the credentials j.matthew@nexus.htb / N27xh!!2ucY04, I successfully logged into the Krayin CRM admin dashboard. Checking the account menu, I confirmed the application was running Krayin CRM v2.2.0. Identifying the Vulnerability A quick search for known vulnerabilities in this version turned up a critical arbitrary file upload / remote code execution flaw. I located a public proof-of-concept exploit on GitHub: https://github.com/sh3llc0d3-0x15/CVE-2026-38526-Exploit Setting Up the Exploit I cloned the repository and installed the required dependencies inside a virtual environment. The script's usage is straightforward: Since the exploit required a payload file, I used the classic PHP reverse shell from pentestmonkey, updating the $ip and $port variables to point back to my attacking machine: https://github.com/pentestmonkey/php-reverse-shell/blob/master/php-reverse-shell.php Shell as www-data With the payload ready, I ran the exploit against the target: I started a listener and triggered the payload by requesting the returned path: http://billing.nexus.htb/storage/tinymce/7126b7043c1212ad9553f29e71b3ded8.php in the browser fired the shell back to my listener. I upgraded the shell to a fully interactive TTY: --- Privilege Escalation Enumerating the home directory, I found two folders: html and krayin. Inside krayin, I listed the full directory contents and found a readable .env file. The .env file contained a database password: I tried this password against the local user jones, and it worked: I confirmed the credentials also worked over SSH: User Flag --- Privilege Escalation: jones → root Enumeration I first checked sudo privileges for jones, which were explicitly denied. I pulled down linpeas.sh for a broader sweep of the system. Key Finding: A Root-Owned systemd Timer Among the active systemd timers, gitea-template-sync.timer stood out — it had run less than a minute prior. This timer fires every minute and triggers gitea-template-sync.service. The corresponding service file revealed it runs as root. Analyzing template-sync.py 1. Loads config — reads GITEA_API_TOKEN from /etc/gitea/template-sync.conf or /opt/forge/app/.env. 2. Queries Gitea's API for repositories, filtering down to those flagged template: true. 3. For each template repo, it runs git ls-tree -r HEAD against the bare repository to enumerate every blob, then extracts each file with git cat-file blob , writing the contents to STAGING_DIR/ / / while preserving the executable bit. 4. Logs everything to /var/log/template-sync.log. The script trusts filepath, as returned by git ls-tree, to be a safe relative path — there is no sanitization or traversal check. Since any authenticated Gitea user can create a repository and flag it as a template, this means any user controls filepath, and therefore controls where root writes files on disk. Building the Exploit Step 1 — Create a template repository. I logged into git.nexus.htb as jones using the password recovered earlier (y27xb3ha!!74GbR) and created a new repository named Exploit owned by jones, with the "Make repository a template" option enabled. Step 2 — Generate an SSH key pair to plant. Step 3 — Clone the new repository. Step 4 — Commit malicious code using low-level Git plumbing. The crafted tree places the public key at authorized_keys using a relative path traversal of the form: ../../../../root/.ssh/authorized_keys The script constructs the blob, builds the nested tree objects, writes a commit pointing at the top-level tree, and updates refs/heads/main accordingly — all using raw Git object construction (hashlib.sha1, zlib.compress) so that git ls-tree on the server returns the traversal path verbatim. Step 5 — Force-push the crafted commit. Browsing the repository on Gitea confirmed the crafted path traversal structure was present in the tree. Root Shell With the key planted, I authenticated over SSH directly as root: Root Flag

structuredData.description: An IDOR vulnerability in a web dashboard leaks FTP credentials captured in a packet dump, leading to user access. From there, a misconfigured Linux capability on the Python binary grants a straightforward path to root.

body: Overview Cap is an Easy-rated Linux machine that centers around two distinct, easy-to-understand misconfigurations rather than any complex exploit chain, making it a great box for beginners learning the basics of web and Linux privilege escalation. The attack path starts with a custom "Security Dashboard" web app on port 80 that auto-logs visitors in as a user named Nathan. A quick look at the app's "Security Snapshot" feature reveals a classic IDOR (Insecure Direct Object Reference) — the download URL references files by a simple incrementing ID, and tweaking that ID exposes a packet capture that was never meant to be accessible. Since FTP (also running on the box) transmits credentials in plaintext, that leaked pcap hands over valid SSH credentials almost immediately. Once on the box as a low-privileged user, privilege escalation to root comes down to a single misconfigured Linux capability: the cap_setuid flag set on the system's Python 3 binary. That one setting lets any user who can run Python call setuid(0) and spawn a root shell — no sudo rights, no kernel exploit, no password needed. In short: web IDOR → leaked creds → user access → abused binary capability → root. Machine Info --- Recon I started, as always, with an Nmap scan to get a picture of what's running on the box. Three open TCP ports. Here's how I prioritized them: - Port 21 (FTP) — I always check for an anonymous login first, since it's one of the most common misconfigurations and takes seconds to rule out. - Port 22 (SSH) — Without credentials or a known username to test, there's nothing to do here yet. I set it aside for later. - Port 80 (HTTP) — A custom "Security Dashboard" application running on Gunicorn. This looked like the most promising entry point, so I focused my enumeration here. FTP: Anonymous Login I tried an anonymous FTP login to rule out the easy win first. No luck — anonymous access was disabled. I moved on to the web application. Web Enumeration Browsing to the web server on port 80 landed me on a Security Dashboard, and interestingly, I was already logged in as a user called Nathan. No login screen, no credentials needed — the session was just handed to me. The dashboard had a feature called "Security Snapshot (5 second PCAP + Analysis)." Clicking it triggered a short network capture and gave me a link to download the result. The URL it generated looked like this: That numeric ID at the end of the URL immediately stood out to me. Whenever an application exposes a resource using a simple, predictable, sequential number like this, it's worth testing whether you can access other resources just by changing that number — a class of vulnerability known as IDOR (Insecure Direct Object Reference). In plain terms: the app isn't properly checking whether the logged-in user is actually allowed to see the file being requested — it just trusts whatever ID is in the URL. To test this, I manually edited the URL to request ID 0 instead of 1: I was still logged in as Nathan, but the file returned was different — meaning the app happily served me a resource that belonged to someone (or something) else entirely. Why I tried ID 0 specifically: On most systems, IDs starting at 0 or 1 represent the earliest or most privileged records created. On Linux, for example, UID 0 is reserved for the root account, while UID 1 is typically the first regular user created after installation. Applying that same logic to this dashboard, ID 0 seemed like a good bet for either the very first capture ever taken, or one tied to an administrative process — and it paid off. Analyzing the Capture The file downloaded from /data/0 was a .pcap (packet capture) file — essentially a recording of network traffic. Since FTP transmits credentials in plaintext (it has no built-in encryption), any login attempt captured in that traffic would be fully readable. I opened the file with strings, a simple command-line tool that pulls out readable text from a binary file — a fast way to eyeball a pcap for anything obviously interesting without firing up Wireshark. Sure enough, buried in the output was a plaintext FTP login — a username and password. Someone (likely an admin testing the dashboard) had authenticated to the box's FTP service while this capture was running, and the dashboard had unintentionally exposed that recording to any logged-in user, including me. Gaining a Foothold: SSH I took the credentials recovered from the pcap and tried them against SSH, since reused credentials across services on the same box are common in these challenges. It worked. I was in as nathan, and the user flag was sitting right there in the home directory. Privilege Escalation With a foothold established, my next goal was root. I started with the basics — checking what Nathan was allowed to run with elevated privileges. No sudo rights. Next stop: LinPEAS, a widely-used enumeration script that automatically scans a Linux box for common privilege escalation vectors (misconfigured permissions, exposed credentials, dangerous capabilities, cron jobs, and so on) so you don't have to check everything by hand. I spun up a quick local Python web server on my attack machine, then pulled linpeas.sh onto the target over HTTP: What LinPEAS Found LinPEAS flagged an interesting Linux capability assigned directly to the Python 3.8 binary. I confirmed it manually with getcap, a tool that lists any special capabilities attached to a binary: This was the key. A quick explanation for anyone unfamiliar with Linux capabilities: normally, only the root user can do powerful, system-level things. Capabilities let you hand out individual pieces of root's power to a specific program, without making that program fully root-owned. It's meant to be a safer, more fine-grained alternative to just running everything as root. In this case, cap_setuid had been granted to the Python binary. This capability allows a process to call setuid() — the system function that changes which user a running process is acting as. Normally, only root can arbitrarily change a process's user ID to anything it wants. But because Python itself had been granted this capability, any script run with this Python binary could call setuid(0) and instantly become root — no exploit needed, no password required. It's effectively an unlocked back door built right into a legitimate system binary. Abusing the Capability I launched Python and used it to spawn a root shell: That was it. os.setuid(0) switched my effective user ID to 0 — root — and pty.spawn("bash") dropped me into a fully interactive root shell. Finally, I grabbed the root flag:

body: Overview Orion is an Easy-difficulty Linux machine built around a Craft CMS 5.6.16 instance exposed on port 80. Enumeration of the site revealed the CMS and version, which had a known exploit available in Metasploit, giving initial access as www-data. From there, a .env file in the Craft installation directory leaked database credentials, which I used to connect directly to the backend MySQL instance and dump the users table. The extracted admin password hash cracked via hashcat against rockyou.txt, yielding valid SSH credentials for the adam user and the user flag. Post-exploitation port enumeration on the box showed two additional services — MySQL (3306) and Telnet (23) — researching the Telnet service pointed to CVE-2026-24061, a telnetd auto-login flaw. Passing a crafted USER environment variable (USER='-f root') alongside the -a flag exploited this trust issue, bypassing authentication entirely and dropping a root shell — completing the box. Machine Info --- Nmap Scan I added the domain and IP to my /etc/hosts file: Port 80 Port 80 leads to a telecom service website. Poking around the site, I found it was powered by Craft CMS. Craft CMS Craft CMS is a flexible, developer-friendly content management system built on PHP. It gives developers a blank canvas for building custom, high-performance sites without locking them into rigid templates or pre-made themes. Nothing else on the front end stood out, so I moved on to directory enumeration. Directory Enumeration with gobuster This turned up http://orion.htb/admin/login. I didn't have credentials, so I tried admin:admin — no luck. The login page did, however, disclose the CMS version: Craft CMS 5.6.16. That gave me a clear next step: check whether this version has any known vulnerabilities. Initial Access I searched for a matching exploit in msfconsole. I set the following options: Running the exploit landed me a shell. Spawning a PTY Shell While exploring the filesystem, I found a .env file under /html/craft: Inside the .env file were the database credentials. Connecting to the Database Using the credentials extracted from the .env file, I connected to the database to harvest further information that might help me escalate to the adam user. I selected the orion database to investigate further. It contained several tables. I focused on the users table and ran a query to pull only the relevant fields: Hash Cracking The hash cracked to: darkangel SSH Connection User Flag Priv Esc --> Root I started by checking for open ports. The machine was listening locally on ports 3306 and 23, both bound to loopback only. To reach them, I set up local port forwarding over my existing SSH session. I focused on port 23 (Telnet) first, since it's historically prone to weak authentication. Research turned up CVE-2026-24061, and I found an Offensive Security article walking through a proof of concept, which I replicated here. Reference: https://www.offsec.com/blog/cve-2026-24061/ Root Flag The vulnerability allowed authentication bypass via the -a auto-login flag combined with a crafted USER environment variable, which the vulnerable telnetd trusted without verifying credentials:

title: Primed for Action
summary: A quick coding challenge solved — filter primes out of a list and multiply them to get the key.

structuredData.headline: Primed for Action
structuredData.description: A quick coding challenge solved — filter primes out of a list and multiply them to get the key.

body: Challenge Scenario: Intelligence units intercepted a list of numbers. Most of them are garbage — but two are prime. Those two primes form a key, obtained by multiplying them together. The goal is to recover that key. Recon Connected to the target over raw TCP: The service serves an in-browser code editor over the socket. Default language was Python, but I switched to C++ since that's what I'm most comfortable with it. Starting Template The challenge hands you this skeleton: It reads a single int n and echoes it straight back — no logic at all. The real input is a list of 50 space-separated integers, so the template needs to be reworked to read an array instead of a scalar. Solution Approach - Read all 50 integers into an array. - isPrime() runs simple trial division up to sqrt(num) — more than enough for numbers in this range. - Multiply every prime found into a running product, using long long to avoid overflow. - Print the final product — that's the key. structuredData.description: DevHub is a Linux machine compromised via CVE-2026-23744, an unauthenticated RCE in MCPJam v1.4.2, followed by lateral movement through an exposed Jupyter Lab instance with a plaintext token, and privilege escalation via a hardcoded API key in an internal Flask service running as root.

body: Summary DevHub is a Linux machine centered around a development environment exposing an MCP (Model Context Protocol) Inspector server. The attack chain starts with exploiting CVE-2026-23744, an unauthenticated RCE in MCPJam v1.4.2, to land a shell as mcp-dev. From there, a Jupyter Lab instance running as analyst is discovered on an internal port — its authentication token is exposed in plaintext via process arguments. Jupyter's REST API and WebSocket protocol are abused to execute code as analyst and read the user flag. Privilege escalation to root comes from a Flask-based internal service (OPSMCP) running as root, whose source code reveals a hardcoded API key and an undocumented admin endpoint that dumps root's SSH private key. --- Machine Info --- Reconnaissance The scan returns two open ports: 22 (SSH) and 80 (HTTP). SSH is a dead end at this stage — no credentials have been found and the machine provides none by default. Port 80 is the entry point. Before proceeding, the target IP is added to /etc/hosts: Note: The redirect operator >> runs as the current user, not as root, so using sudo echo ... >> /etc/hosts fails. tee -a is the correct approach since it runs under sudo. --- Web Enumeration The landing page on port 80 lists three internal platforms: - MCP Inspector — active on port 6274 - Analytics Dashboard — internal only, localhost:8888 - Code Repository — internal Git server MCP Inspector Navigating to the MCP Inspector and checking the settings tab reveals the server version: MCPJam v1.4.2. A quick search for this version reveals a critical unauthenticated RCE vulnerability: CVE-2026-23744. The advisory is documented at https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-232v-j27c-5pp6. The root cause is that the MCP Inspector accepts arbitrary command and args via its /api/mcp/connect endpoint and spawns them as a child process without any validation or authentication. By default, it also binds to 0.0.0.0 instead of 127.0.0.1, making it externally reachable. --- Foothold Setting Up the Listener Crafting the Payload Direct use of shell redirects (>&) in the JSON payload can cause issues because /dev/tcp is a bash-only feature — it does not exist in sh. To work around this, the reverse shell command is base64-encoded and piped through bash at execution time: The outer shell (sh -c) decodes and pipes the payload into bash, ensuring /dev/tcp is interpreted correctly. Triggering RCE Initial Shell as mcp-dev A reverse shell lands as mcp-dev. The shell is then stabilized using Python's pty module: Landing directory: /opt/mcpjam/node_modules/@mcpjam/inspector --- Lateral Movement Process Enumeration With a foothold on the box, internal services are enumerated to find paths to other users: Two services are found running on loopback (127.0.0.1), inaccessible externally but reachable from the current shell: - Port 8888 — Jupyter Lab running as analyst - Port 5000 — OPSMCP Flask server running as root Jupyter Lab is the immediate target since it runs as analyst and its authentication token is visible in plaintext in the process arguments — a consequence of how Jupyter passes the token as a CLI flag at startup. Confirming Jupyter Access The extracted token is used to verify API access and list available notebooks: Response confirms one notebook: quarterly_analysis.ipynb. The API is live and the token is valid. Creating a Kernel Jupyter's code execution model works in two stages: first a kernel (Python interpreter) is created via the REST API, then code is sent to it over a WebSocket connection. The kernel runs as the user who owns the Jupyter process — in this case, analyst. Response: Executing Code via WebSocket Jupyter does not accept code execution over HTTP — all kernel communication happens over WebSocket on the /api/kernels/ /channels endpoint. Since websocket-client was not available on the machine, the WebSocket handshake and frame format are implemented manually using raw sockets. WebSocket frame structure (client → server): - 0x81 — FIN bit set, opcode 1 (text frame) - Length byte(s) — 1 byte for ≤125, 3 bytes for ≤65535, 9 bytes for larger - 4-byte masking key — client-to-server frames must be masked per RFC 6455 - Masked payload — each byte XOR'd with the corresponding masking key byte --- User Flag --- Privilege Escalation Reading the MCP Source The Flask service on port 5000 runs as root and requires an X-API-Key header. Direct file access to /opt/opsmcp/server.py is not available as mcp-dev, but the Jupyter kernel running as analyst can read it. It accepts target=ssh_keys and reads /root/.ssh/id_rsa directly, since the process runs as root. This is a classic security-through-obscurity failure: the endpoint is undocumented but fully functional and unprotected beyond the shared API key. Dumping the Root SSH Key The response contains root's RSA private key. body: Lab-Setup: Both the machines are configured on NAT Network. Nmap Scan: The host was confirmed to be alive and reachable, with minimal latency observed. Out of 65,535 TCP ports, only three ports were found open, indicating a relatively small external attack surface. Identified Services - Port 22/tcp — SSH - Port 53/tcp — DNS - Port 80/tcp — HTTP Host Information - Operating System: Linux - MAC Address: 08:00:27:AF:9D:B3 - Virtualization: Oracle VirtualBox (virtual NIC detected) The target system exposes SSH, DNS, and HTTP services. While the number of open ports is limited, multiple services disclose version information, which can be leveraged for version-specific vulnerability research. Further enumeration of the web server and authentication mechanisms is recommended. Web Enumeration: An nginx web server running on port 80. Accessing the service displayed the default nginx welcome page. Directory busting I performed directory brute-forcing against the web server using ffuf with the directory-list-2.3-medium.txt wordlist. The scan returned mostly false positives caused by the web server responding with identical content for non-existent paths. One valid directory was identified: - /secret — HTTP 200 When I navigated to /secret, the server initiated a file download. No! exploitable web directories or application endpoints were identified through directory busting. Based on the result, I did DNS reconnaissance. DNS reconnaissance revealed that the target IP resolves to the hostname blackpearl.tcm. I then added the domain mapping to my local hosts file, resolving blackpearl.tcm to the target IP address. Web Enumeration (Virtual Host) After updating the local hosts file, I accessed http://blackpearl.tcm and observed that the application served a PHP-based web page. - PHP Version: 7.3.27-1~deb10u1 Directory Fuzzing (Virtual Host) I then again performed directory enumeration against http://blackpearl.tcm using Gobuster to confirm whether any hidden application paths were present. The scan identified a single accessible directory: - /navigate — HTTP 301 (redirects to /navigate/) Navigating to this path revealed that the web application is running a content management system (CMS). Application Identification The application was identified as: - Navigate CMS v2.8 With the CMS and version confirmed, I conducted targeted vulnerability research. Public exploit research revealed the existence of a Metasploit proof-of-concept module for unauthorized remote code execution (RCE) affecting this version of Navigate CMS. Rapid7 Exploitation — Navigate CMS v2.8 I loaded the following Metasploit module: - exploit/multi/http/navigate_cms_rce The exploit was configured to target the CMS installation located at /navigate/ and to use the correct virtual host blackpearl.tcm. Once the required options were set, I executed the exploit. The module successfully bypassed authentication, uploaded a malicious payload, and triggered execution on the target system. Once the required options were set, I executed the exploit. The module successfully bypassed authentication, uploaded a malicious payload, and triggered execution on the target system. obtained a Meterpreter reverse shell. Initial Access Confirmation After spawning a shell from the Meterpreter session, I verified the execution context: - User: www-data This confirmed that I had achieved remote code execution as the web server user, indicating successful initial foothold but with limited privileges. At this stage, privilege escalation was required to gain root-level access and retrieve the target flag. Spawning a TTY shell This resulted in a stable interactive shell as www-data, enabling reliable execution of enumeration and privilege escalation techniques. Privilege Escalation After gaining an initial foothold as www-data, I proceeded with local privilege escalation enumeration using LinPEAS. I hosted the LinPEAS script on my attacking machine and transferred it to the target: On the target system, I downloaded the script to /tmp: With the script successfully transferred, I executed LinPEAS to identify potential privilege escalation vectors. SUID Enumeration LinPEAS revealed the presence of multiple SUID binaries. To validate this, I manually enumerated SUID files: Notable SUID binaries included: - /usr/bin/php7.3 - /usr/bin/su - /usr/bin/passwd - /usr/bin/mount - /usr/bin/umount The presence of php7.3 with the SUID bit set stood out as a high-risk misconfiguration. SUID Abuse via PHP I researched the identified SUID binaries on GTFOBins and confirmed that PHP can be abused to spawn a shell while preserving elevated privileges. I executed the following command to spawn a privileged shell: - Effective UID (euid): root - Real UID: www-data This indicated successful privilege escalation, allowing access to root-owned files and directories. Root Access & Flag Retrieval With root privileges effectively obtained, I accessed the root directory and retrieved the flag: Blackpearl successfully rooted 😎

body: Lab Setup: Both the machine are on a NAT Network. --- Pinging: To verify that the target system was reachable. Service & Port Enumeration (Nmap) The scan confirms that the target is a Windows-based system exposing several standard Windows services. Ports 135, 139, and 445 are open, indicating the presence of RPC and SMB, which are common enumeration and attack vectors on Windows environments. In addition, a web service is accessible on port 8080, running Jetty 9.4.41. This immediately stands out as a potential entry point, as custom or misconfigured web applications often provide an initial foothold. The presence of a robots.txt file suggests hidden or restricted paths that warrant further investigation. SMB enumeration scripts also revealed the NetBIOS name “BUTLER”, confirming the machine identity. Based on these findings, further enumeration was focused on the web application on port 8080 and SMB services. Port 8080: Web Application (Jenkins) Accessing the web service on port 8080 revealed a Jenkins login interface, indicating the presence of a Jenkins automation server exposed to the network. Since Jenkins commonly runs with elevated privileges and supports script execution through build pipelines, it represents a high-value attack surface. Misconfigurations such as weak credentials, anonymous access, or vulnerable plugins can often lead to remote code execution. Based on this discovery, further enumeration was focused on Jenkins authentication mechanisms and configuration. Jenkins Authentication Bypass (Brute Force) I targeted the Jenkins login endpoint using Burp Suite Intruder to test common credential combinations. A cluster bomb attack was configured against the j_username and j_password parameters. During the attack, I identified valid credentials: - Username: jenkins - Password: jenkins This confirmed that Jenkins was exposed with weak/default credentials, granting me unauthorized access to the administrative interface. Post-Authentication Access After successfully logging in, I gained access to the Jenkins dashboard. While reviewing the available features, I identified functionality that allows script execution, indicating a clear path to remote code execution. Given Jenkins’ ability to execute scripts and jobs with elevated privileges, this presented an opportunity to obtain a reverse shell and establish an initial foothold on the target system. Remote Code Execution via Jenkins (Groovy Script) https://gist.github.com/frohoff/fed1ffaab9b9beeb1c76 After gaining access to the Jenkins dashboard, I searched for a Groovy-based reverse shell payload suitable for execution through Jenkins’ script functionality. I found a publicly available Groovy reverse shell script and adapted it to my listener configuration. I executed the script through Jenkins, which resulted in a successful callback to my machine. Privilege Escalation Enumeration with winPEAS.exe After establishing an initial foothold on the machine, the next objective was to identify potential privilege escalation vectors. Given that Butler is a Windows-based target, I opted to use winPEAS.exe. With winPEASx64.exe downloaded on the Kali attacking machine, I transferred the binary to the compromised Butler host for local execution. During local enumeration with winPEAS, I identified a vulnerable Windows service named WiseBootAssistant (Wise Care 365). The service was running with elevated privileges and had an unquoted executable path containing spaces, making it susceptible to an unquoted service path attack. Payload Generation I generated a malicious executable on Kali using msfvenom to obtain a reverse shell. Payload Transfer The payload was transferred to the vulnerable directory using certutil: Service Restart and Escalation I restarted the vulnerable service to trigger execution of the malicious binary: got the shell (but not Administrator)

body: Lab Setup: Both the target machine (DEV) and the attacker machine (Kali Linux) are configured on the same NAT network. Kali Linux Dev --- Pinging A successful ping confirms that the attacker machine can communicate with the target machine. Nmap Scan The target machine has the following important ports open: - 'Port 22 (SSH)' SSH service is running. - 'Port 80 (HTTP)' Apache 2.4 web server is running and serving a Bolt installation error page. - 'Port 2049 (NFS)' NFS (Network File Share) service is active. - 'Port 8080 (HTTP)' Hosting a PHP info page. Port 2049 I checked if the NFS share was accessible to my machine and to identify what directories I could potentially mount and extract files from. There is an NFS directory being shared, so to access its contents, I first created a local directory to mount it. I mounted the target’s NFS share to this directory The -t option specifies the filesystem type, which in this case is NFS. I found a save.zip file inside the mounted directory. When I attempted to unzip it, it prompted for a password. The file preview showed that it contains two files: id_rsa and todo.txt. To recover the password and extract the contents, I used fcrackzip to perform a password‑cracking attack on save.zip. zip file password crack -v → verbosity -u → unzip -D → dictionary attack -p → attack against a file The attack was successful, and the password was revealed as: java101. I then unzipped the file and viewed its contents. The todo.txt file contains: Since I didn’t know the correct username, trying to establish an SSH connection using the id_rsa key was not useful. Because of that, I moved on to checking the other open ports to look for leads. Port 80 it shows that the database and the config directory is accessible openly and these directory have confidential information in it. I downloaded the config.yml file and it had a pair of username and password Port 8080 At the /dev there is a page. After registering, I explored the interface but didn’t find anything useful. Since nothing on the page appeared exploitable, I searched online for publicly known vulnerabilities or CVEs related to BoltWire. I found a Local File Inclusion (LFI) exploit at: BoltWire 6.03 - Local File Inclusion The exploit worked and returned the contents of the '/etc/passwd' file. From this output, I identified a user named jeanpaul on the system. Now that I know the username '(jeanpaul)' and have the 'id_rsa' private key, I’ll attempt to establish an SSH connection to the target. Exploitation: The passphrase for the id_rsa key was I_love_java which I previously found in the config.yml file After logging in, the first step was to check which commands the user can run with elevated privileges. The user has permission to run the zip command with elevated privileges, so I checked https://gtfobins.github.io/ for a privilege‑escalation method using this command. These commands worked, and I successfully gained root access. Flag Flag captured. System owned. 🎯

body: Lab Setup: Both the machine are on a NAT Network. Academy Kali-Linux Pinging To verify that the target machine was reachable from my attacking machine, I began by checking connectivity. If the host doesn’t respond to basic network checks, the assessment cannot proceed. Nmap Scan: Nmap scan revealed three open ports: FTP (21), SSH (22), and HTTP (80). The FTP service was running vsftpd 3.0.3 and allowed anonymous login (FTP code 230). Inside the FTP directory, there is a note.txt, which appeared accessible without authentication. Before moving forward with deeper enumeration, I decided to retrieve and review this file, as such notes often provide useful clues or misconfigurations that can be leveraged later in the attack chain. FTP I downloaded the 'note.txt' file from the FTP server to inspect its contents and determine whether it contained any useful information get the note.txt file contents of the note.txt file key information from the note.txt password hash cd73502828457d15655bbd7a63fb0bc8 student name Rum Ham The note.txt file contained several pieces of information that were immediately relevant. It included a password hash (cd73502828457d15655bbd7a63fb0bc8), the student name ‘Rum Ham’, and a roll number of 10201321. I noted these details for potential use during authentication or user‑based enumeration later in the assessment. Identify the hash This is a MD5 hash Crack the hash the password is student Web enumeration The HTTP service only displayed the default Apache page, which indicated poor server hygiene and suggested that the organization had left services exposed without proper configuration. This indicates the pentester to look deeper into the web directory and underlying application structure. Directory enumeration Directory enumeration revealed two accessible paths: '/academy' and '/phpadmin'. /academy Navigating to '/academy' redirected me to a CMS login page. title: EternalBlue (MS17-010) — Windows 7 SP1 Exploitation Walkthrough
summary: Compromise of a Windows 7 SP1 lab machine by exploiting the MS17-010 EternalBlue SMB vulnerability via Metasploit to obtain a SYSTEM-level Meterpreter shell and extract password hashes, followed by a manual exploitation attempt using AutoBlue that resulted in a BSOD.

body: Lab Setup Both machines are configured on a NAT network. Kali Linux Windows --- Pinging Verified connectivity by pinging the target from the Kali host to confirm the device was reachable. Nmap Scan: The target 10.0.2.5 is up and identified as Windows 7 Ultimate (6.1.7601 SP1). Open, relevant services: SMB/RPC accessible on 135, 139, 445 (microsoft-ds/NetBIOS/RPC) and RDP (3389); the RDP service presents an SSL certificate for WIN-845Q99OO4PP valid 2025-10-15 → 2026-04-16 and reports Product_Version: 6.1.7601. SMB scripts show the scanner accessed SMB as guest, authentication level user, challenge/response supported, and message signing is disabled / not required, which weakens integrity protections. Service detection and SMB OS discovery consistently return the Windows 7 SP1 fingerprint and workgroup WORKGROUP. Exploitation using Metasploit Searched for 'ernalblue' on msfconsole The exploitation was performed using the Metasploit module 'exploit/windows/smb/ms17_010_eternalblue' Set options Exploit It worked and I got the meterpreter shell Hashdump - Those lines from hashdump are password hashes extracted from the Windows. Format: username:RID:LM_HASH:NTLM_HASH:::. - The NTLM_HASH values are what an attacker would target to recover plaintext passwords via offline cracking. Whether cracking succeeds depends on password strength and attacker resources. - Possession of these hashes is evidence of credential exposure and a serious security breach. --- Manual Exploitation I searched for public exploits avaliable for the eternal blue and found this github repo with detailed walkthrough https://github.com/3ndG4me/AutoBlue-MS17-010 Clone the repo Install the requirements Usage ./shell_prep.sh ./listener_prep.sh Exploit The exploit crashed the target machine, resulting in the Blue screen:

structuredData.description: Compromise of a VulnHub Linux machine by enumerating an exposed Samba 2.2.1a service, identifying the trans2open buffer overflow vulnerability, and exploiting it via Metasploit to obtain a root shell directly.

body: Nmap Scan: It exposes SSH (port 22 — OpenSSH 2.9p2, SSHv1 supported, weak 1024-bit keys), HTTP/HTTPS (ports 80/443 — Apache 1.3.20 with mod_ssl/OpenSSL 0.9.6b, SSLv2 enabled and expired cert), SMB/NetBIOS on 139 (Samba smbd, workgroup MYGROUP), and RPC services on 111/32768 (rpcbind/status). I will proceed to enumerate the SMB service. Enumerating SMB The Metasploit scan identified the target running Samba version 2.2.1a on a Unix system. Searchsploit — Samba 2.2 Exploit Candidates I ran searchsploit Samba 2.2 and found multiple ExploitDB PoCs and Metasploit modules for Samba 2.2-era vulnerabilities (.rb = Metasploit module; .c/.pl/.py/.txt = standalone PoC). I’ll pick the exploit that matches the target’s OS/arch/version for testing. call_trans2open processes TRANS2_OPEN SMB requests; flawed parsing there causes buffer/heap overflows that can lead to remote code execution. It’s critical because SMB is network-exposed and the same handler was vulnerable across multiple OSes, so many PoCs target that routine. Metasploit — call_trans2open module I inspected the call_trans2open Metasploit module, confirmed it targets Samba 2.2.x TRANS2_OPEN, and will set RHOSTS/RPORT to test SMB in a controlled lab. \\\\ I chose the Linux call_trans2open exploit for Samba 2.2.x (based on Nmap showing a Linux host). It’s attempted a brute‑force attack that iterated through multiple target addresses ie; the selected payload did not execute successfully. I searched for a Linux x86 reverse, non‑staged payload for the exploit. Exploiting 🥳 I got a root shell on kioptrix.level1.

Add the domain to /etc/hosts: Web Enumeration: Directory Discovery: index.php: I browsed to http://soulmate.htb. The site presented a signup/login page. I created a new account, signed up successfully, and then logged in to access the main application area. This yielded nothing useful, so I moved on to subdomain enumeration. Sub-Domian Discovery: - ftp.soulmate.htb exists as a virtual-hosted site on that IP (or at least the server handles that Host header). - A 302 usually means redirect — could be to a login page, another hostname, or an internal path. The empty body suggests the server returns just headers. - This is worth investigating: could be an admin panel, service landing page, or an intentional redirect to external resource. I added ftp.soulmate.htb in my /etc/hosts file against the machine ip. I visited the http://ftp.soulmate.htb I tried loggin with the common default creds as well as the creds set on the \\http://soulmate.htb\\ but it didn’t worked. I then Looked the soorce and found the version of the WebInterface Version : 11.W.657-2025_03_08_07_52 Exploit : I searched for the exploit for the specific version I looked for a public CVE exploit and found a relevant GitHub repository. https://github.com/Immersive-Labs-Sec/CVE-2025-31161 I cloned the repo Usage: Exploitation: Login Creds = b3ta-blocker : hello_World Successful Login: I opened User Manager, saw I could change any user’s password, changed ben’s password, and then login into ben’s account with the new credentials. I Logedin the ben user account While exploring Ben’s account, I noticed an option to upload files into the WebProb directory. I used the GitHub repo to prepare a shell.php reverse shell, uploaded it to the WebProbdirectory, started a listener on my machine, then accessed the uploadedshell.php to get a reverse shell. GitHub - pentestmonkey/php-reverse-shell Before uploading, open the php file and replace the placeholder LHOST/LPORT with your machine's IP and listener port. File Upload: Before running curl, make sure your listener is started and actively listening for connections. Got the reverse Shell. I didn’t have sudo access (so sudo -l wasn’t available) and there were no cronjobs (crontab returned nothing). I then downloaded linpeas.sh into /tmp. body: Machine information: --- Pinging: The target machine is inside my local network, now I can move forward with network scanning to discover services, or open ports in the same network. After scanning, I can continue with enumeration (collecting detailed information about the system and services) and then attempt privilege escalation to gain full root access Nmap Scan: - Port 22 (SSH) → Keep in mind for later privilege escalation or login once creds are found. - Port 1234 → Looks restricted, may require deeper probing. - Port 8000 → Main focus now — web application likely vulnerable. Port 8000: The first step after finding a web service is to browse the website normally, just like an everyday user. While doing this, I also keep Burp Suite running in the background to capture all the requests and responses. This helps me spot anything unusual or sensitive (like hidden parameters, tokens, or errors) that might give me leads for further enumeration. On this site, I noticed there are Register and Login buttons. So, I created a new account by registering, and then logged in to see how the application behaves and what features are available. After logging in, I was presented with a code editor interface, very similar to the one from the previous HackTheBox machine “Code”_. Code-HackThBox This editor is a JavaScript editor instead of Python like before. My first step is to test the editor and see what kind of code execution it allows. I’m also assuming there will be filters or restrictions in place (just like in the earlier machine) to prevent direct exploitation. After trying many approaches and searching extensively, I initially focused on bypassing JavaScript filters. Most of the guides I found were about web-based JavaScript injection, which wasn’t applicable here. In this challenge, the goal is to execute code directly in the JavaScript editor, which is a different scenario than typical JS injection on web pages. After struggling for a while, I came across John Hammond’s video on escaping JavaScript sandboxes, which provided the correct approach for this type of environment. Next, I decided to download the application as a ZIP file to inspect its source code and structure. Inside the code, particularly in app.py, I noticed it was using the js2py library. This library allows running JavaScript code from Python. I then looked for possible vulnerabilities or existing exploits. I found a CVE related to js2py, but many proof-of-concept scripts didn’t work for this setup. Finally, I came across a GitHub repository with a working method for this type of exploitation. Using that approach, I inserted my reverse shell into the code editor, executed it, and successfully got a shell on the target machine. https://github.com/waleed-hassan569/CVE-2024-28397-command-execution-poc/blob/main/payload.js Script: Reverse Shell I executed the reverse shell, and it worked successfully. This gave me a shell on the target machine. Make the Shell Stable: I checked the shell I got, but it had very limited access and didn’t contain anything useful. To progress, I need to migrate to another user with more privileges or useful files. While exploring the system, I found a home directory for a user named marco, which could be the next target. I wanted to get the password for the marco user. Since I had previously downloaded the application and was familiar with its file structure, I knew where to look. I went directly to the instance directory and found a file called user.db. I then checked this database file to see if it contained any user information or credentials. marco’s hash : 649c9d65a206a75f5abe509fe128bce5 password : sweetangelbabylove SSH login User Flag: User Flag : ab17d77653f9d09b9c693554b26eaa4b Root Flag: It has npbackup-cli installed, which is a command-line backup tool. It functions similarly to other backup utilities like restic, allowing users to create, manage, and restore backups of directories and files. In this scenario, since the marco have sudo privileges on npbackup-cli, it’s possible to use it to read or back up files that are normally restricted, including root-owned files. This means I can potentially use npbackup-cli to back up the root directory and extract sensitive files, such as root.txt, to obtain the root flag — effectively achieving privilege escalation. I didn’t have the permissions to directly edit the original config file for npbackup-cli. So instead, I: 1. Copied the content of the original config file. 2. Created a new file called my.conf. 3. Pasted the copied content into this new file. This allowed me to modify the backup path (e.g., to /root) without needing direct access to the original configuration file. In the npbackup-cli configuration file, I modified the backup path to point to /root. This way, when the backup command is run, it will attempt to back up the root directory, including sensitive files like root.txt, which contains the root flag. Root Flag : 4aff940b07fccd30e5972c5ba9075f6a

Since the machine does not provide any default login username or password (credentials) for SSH, I will first check what is available on the web service (the website running on port 80). Web Enumeration We can use whatweb to try to identify the web application in use. The target runs GetSimple CMS on Apache/2.4.41 (Ubuntu). I added the name gettingstarted.htb to the /etc/hosts file on my system, linking it to the machine’s IP address. It loads now properly I didn’t find anything interesting by browsing the website manually. So now, I’ll use Gobuster to do directory enumeration. This means Gobuster will automatically try lots of possible folder and page names (like /admin, /login, /uploads) to see if the website is hiding any useful pages that I couldn’t find on my own. I ran Gobuster with the common.txt wordlist against http://gettingstarted.htb/ to look for hidden directories. The results showed some interesting findings: - /admin → Redirects to the admin login page. - /backups → Might contain sensitive files or old data. - /data → Could store important information like logs or uploads. - /plugins → May reveal installed plugins that can be exploited. - /robots.txt & /sitemap.xml → Give clues about the site’s structure. - /server-status and hidden files like .htaccess / .htpasswd exist but are blocked (403). I checked the /data page. Inside, I found some the following: the username is admin and the password hash is d033e22ae348aeb5660fc2140aec35850c4da997 Hash crack Login credentials for the /admin page is admin:admin This means I can now log into the /admin page using these credentials and gain access to the website’s admin panel. I used the credentials admin:admin on the /admin page, and they worked. I was able to log in successfully as the admin user. After logging in, I explored the website like a normal user to understand its features and behavior. During this process, I found an upload functionality. This is important because if the upload feature is not properly secured, I can try to upload a malicious file (like a reverse shell). If it works and the file isn’t filtered, I’ll gain a reverse shell connection to the target machine. From there, I can continue with enumeration (collecting more system information) and eventually attempt privilege escalation to gain full control. I ran the sudo -l command to check what privileges the www-data user has. The output showed that www-data can run /usr/bin/php as root without needing a password (NOPASSWD). Nothing interesting here! But I’ll check the /nibbleblog/ I discovered that the website is running on a platform called Nibbleblog. I searched on Google to see if there are any publicly available exploits I found an exploit that looks like it could work. i don’t know the Nibbleblog version, so now, I’ll use a tool called Gobuster. Gobuster is like an automatic scanner that tries lots of different words to guess hidden folders or pages on the website (for example: /admin, /login, /backup). This process is called directory enumeration, and it helps uncover parts of the website that aren’t normally visible through browsing. The scan found some important hidden pages on the website, such as /admin and /admin.php. But before checking those, I’ll first look at the /README page. The /README page confirmed that the application’s version is 4.0.3. This is important because the exploit I found earlier is designed to work on this version. The exploit takes advantage of a weakness in the file upload feature, which means I can try to upload a malicious file to gain access. CVE-2025–24071 — NTLM Hash Leak via .library-ms File Vulnerability Summary: A specially crafted .library-ms file can be used to silently leak NTLM hashes when a user extracts it from a ZIP archive and views it in Windows Explorer. This happens without execution, clicks, or warnings — due to how Windows handles Library files and network shares. Why It Works: 1. '.library-ms' files are legitimate XML-based files that define "Libraries" (e.g., Documents). 2. These can reference remote paths, like \\\\10.10.16.54\\share. 3. When Windows Explorer renders a .library-ms, it tries to load content from the remote path. 4. To access that UNC path, Windows sends NTLM authentication (username + NTLMv2 challenge-response) automatically. 5. If the attacker controls that UNC path (via Metasploit or Responder), they catch the NTLM hash. Exploitation Flow: 1. Attacker creates a malicious .library-ms that points to \\\\attacker-ip\\share. 2. Packs it into a exploit.zip. 3. Victim extracts the zip using Windows Explorer. 4. Windows automatically renders the .library-ms, triggering a connection to the remote SMB path. 5. Windows sends NTLM credentials silently to the attacker. 6. Attacker receives and cracks the hash — or reuses it for access. Why ZIP Extraction Is Key: - If .library-ms is downloaded directly, SmartScreen blocks it. - If it’s extracted from a zip, Windows treats it as local and auto-renders without warning. - This bypasses security checks and triggers the NTLM leak. Components Involved: Mitigation: - Patch (when released) - Block outbound SMB (ports 445, 139) - Disable NTLM auth where possible - Educate users: Don’t open random ZIPs - Use Smart App Control or attack surface reduction rules Real-World Use Case: - Delivered via phishing (ZIP with .library-ms) - Uploaded to exposed shares (as you did via SMB) - Triggers automatically on folder view - Used by APTs to steal domain hashes for lateral movement CVE-2025–24071 exploits the way Windows Explorer renders .library-ms files by tricking it into silently leaking NTLM hashes when the file is extracted from a ZIP archive and viewed — no clicks needed. --- Then following the commands i created the exploit under the name of "exploit.zip" and then used the "put command" to send it to the target device for execution 😞 No module was there so had to clone the repository Now the exploit is there and ready to be used! I then set the target IP and verified that everything is configured correctly: Directed to the Desktop directory and ran the module to get the .zip file: Now I'll put the exploit on the target device: I also set up a listener: I got the username and its NTLM hash: - username = p.agila - NTLM hash = p.agila::FLUFFY:fdc1aa73c3acdb83:B606E98CB19FCB3577179082F267FF74:... I cracked the hash using John the Ripper: password = prometheusx-303 BloodHound Enumeration Looking for relationships in BloodHound: I found this exploit to add a user to the Service Accounts group. AddMember This abuse can be carried out when controlling an object that has a GenericAll, GenericWrite, Self, AllExtendedRights or Self-Membership, over the target group. The command I used: So p.agila is now a member of Service Accounts. The outbound of Service Accounts has GenericWrite to three users, so p.agila also has GenericWrite access. I now need to abuse this. The GenericWrite permission in Active Directory allows a user to modify all writable attributes of an object, except for properties that require special permissions such as resetting passwords.
